newsitem.title: ITALY: OECD sees Italy 1997 deficit/GDP at 3.2 pct.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees Italy 1997 deficit/GDP at 3.2 pct.

text.p: Italy's public deficit in 1997 will fall to 3.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from 6.7 percent in 1996, leaving it just outside the Maastricht Treaty criteria for the single currency, the OECD said on Thursday.
The twice-yearly Economic Outlook report by the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development also forecast Italy's public deficit/GDP ratio would widen to 3.8 percent in 1998.

The Maastricht criteria for European nations wishing to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU) at its start in January 1999 stipulate governments must bring their 1997 budget deficits down to around three percent of total output.

"The 1997 budget and subsequent mini-budget together with the associated convergence of interest rates have significantly increased the possibility of bringing the deficit down to the Maastricht limit in 1997," the report said.

But it warned the budget deficit will rise steeply again in 1998 to significantly above the target. Sustainably reducing the ratio will require structural reform of pensions and other welfare programmes to be accelerated, the OECD said.

The Italian government has targeted a budget deficit/GDP ratio of 3.0 percent in 1997, while its three-year 1998-2000 economic plan (DPEF) unveiled last month sees the ratio at just 2.8 percent in 1998, 2.4 percent in 1999 and 1.8 percent in the year 2000.

Italy's centre-left government led by Romano Prodi has staked its reputation on fulfilling the Maastricht criteria and joining the single currency at its scheduled start. It has introduced tough deficit-cutting budget measures to cut the deficit/GDP ratio to 3.0 percent in 1997.
The OECD report said that its projections were based on assumptions which included this year's Italian Eurotax and the mini-budget approved by parliament in May.

The widening of the deficit/GDP ratio in 1998 is brought about by the expiry of one-off measures like the Eurotax, which will outweigh cyclical revenue gains and savings in interest payments, the report added.
The OECD said that leading economic indicators point to a mild pick-up in activity in 1997, but it sees real Italian GDP growth limited to around one percent, rising to nearer two percent in 1998.
The government in its DPEF sees real GDP growth of 1.2 percent in 1997, rising to 2.0 percent in 1998.
The report sees Italian consumer price (CPI) inflation falling to two percent in 1997, below the government's target of 2.5 percent.
Italy CPI inflation in May was running at 1.7 percent for the year. The DPEF sees its 2.5 percent 1997 target falling to 1.8 percent in 1998.
